Bay County by the numbers

Which offices touch a Bay County tax bill?

A Bay County bill passes through three sets of hands: an assessor in your own township or city, that unit's treasurer, and later, if the bill goes unpaid, the County Treasurer. County government is built on 14 townships and 4 cities with roughly 102,000 residents, and the county's own about page says tax assessment mostly belongs to those local units.

Between them sits the Equalization Department, which audits fairness across units. According to its duties page, staff study sales and appraisals class by class in every local unit so that assessments stay near 49 to 50 percent of value countywide. The same office drafts the Millage Reduction Report. Your parcel's individual value is left to the local assessor.

  • Assessor: places the value on your parcel and sends the change notice. The county publishes a contact list covering each township and city.
  • Township or city treasurer: mails the July and December bills and takes the first payment.
  • County Treasurer: picks up delinquent real property tax, certifies deeds, and sits as chair of the Land Bank Authority.
  • Equalization: keeps parcel ownership and land description records for most of Bay County. Bangor Township, Hampton Township, Bay City and Essexville keep their own descriptions.

When do Bay County bills arrive and where do payments go?

Bills go out in July and again in December from the township or city treasurer. Any balance that remains with that local treasurer after February 28 is handed to the County Treasurer, and MCL 211.78 sets the rules for collecting it from there.

The County Treasurer's counter is on the sixth floor of the Bay County Building, 515 Center Ave., downtown Bay City. Staff are there weekdays, 8 a.m. through 5 p.m., and the main number is 989-895-4285. The table lists each way the office accepts payment on delinquent accounts.

Payment channels at the Bay County Treasurer. Source: Bay County Treasurer payment options page.
ChannelDetail from the county
By mailAccepts check, card or ACH. To earn that month's payoff figure, the payment must be received by the last business day or postmarked on the month's final day.

The county warns against emailing card numbers or ACH forms, since email is not secure. Mail, fax or phone them in.

What is the route for disputing a Bay County valuation?

Your first stop is the local board of review. State law (MCL 211.30) schedules its opening session for the second Monday of March, though a township or city may choose the Tuesday or Wednesday that follows. During that week the board has to hold at least 12 hours of hearings, including three evening hours after 6 p.m.

Anyone who files a protest must receive a written outcome by the first Monday in June, along with a notice about going further to the Michigan Tax Tribunal. For a house, a tribunal petition is due on July 31 of the tax year. Commercial and industrial owners face May 31 (MCL 205.735a). A homeowner generally has to raise the issue at the board of review before the tribunal will take it.

  • Phone your unit's assessor and ask whether a letter protest is allowed in place of an appearance.
  • Pick up your appraisal record card from the township or city, because the county Equalization office says those cards are kept locally.
  • Use Equalization for parcel ownership, descriptions and tax data. It is staffed Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. through 4 p.m.

A fight over a principal residence exemption starts at the July or December board of review, then may reach the tribunal.

Does Bay County offer property tax relief?

The Equalization site explains a disabled veteran exemption. A veteran needs only one of three qualifications: a federal ruling of permanent and total service connected disability paid at 100 percent, a certificate showing aid for specially adapted housing, or an unemployability rating.

The unremarried surviving spouse keeps the benefit as long as that spouse lives in Michigan. Each year the owner files an affidavit and the federal documents with the local assessor. The filing window opens on tax day and closes when the local board of review adjourns for good.

If you simply cannot cover a bill, call the County Treasurer before the February 28 handoff and ask what options exist. The Land Bank Authority is another resource. The Board of Commissioners created it on August 11, 2009 to take on odd property problems and parcels that do not sell at a public auction.

How does unpaid tax affect a sale of a Bay County house?

Back taxes stay with the land, so a seller settles them at or before the closing table. Michigan's MCL 211.135 has the register of deeds ask for tax certification on warranty deeds, land contracts and condominium master deeds, showing five years of paid tax before the instrument date. Bay County's certificate costs $5, handed over on its own check to the County Treasurer.

A quitclaim deed without a warranty covenant is excused from that step. Even so, most lenders and title companies still want the tax history clean. Have the closing agent request a payoff from the treasurer ahead of the signing date.

For parcels in delinquency, the county treasurer is the foreclosing governmental unit. MCL 211.78 says forfeited property can face a foreclosure judgment if nobody redeems it. An owner with arrears should call the treasurer well before any notice shows up.

Recording the deed also brings transfer tax. The Register of Deeds shows $7.50 for every $1,000 of price to the state and $1.10 per $1,000 to the county. Applied to the $152,200 Census median home value, that is about $1,141 plus $167, near $1,309 in all.

What does Census data show about homes in Bay County?

QuickFacts credits Bay County with 102,123 residents in 2025, which is 1.7 percent fewer than the April 2020 base, spread over 442 square miles of land. Housing totals 48,704 units for 45,103 households, and owners live in 77.0 percent of occupied homes.

For 2020 to 2024 the middle owner occupied home is valued at $152,200, and the middle household earns $61,763. Mortgage holders spend a median $1,249 a month on housing costs, against $557 for owners with no loan. Nearly one resident in four, 24.2 percent, is 65 or older, so exemption timing and downsizing sales come up often.

More questions about Bay County, MI Property Tax Guide

After what date do Bay County property taxes move to the county?

A balance still open with the township or city treasurer on February 28 passes to the Bay County Treasurer, under MCL 211.78. Call 989-895-4285 to get a payoff number.

Is paying a Bay County property tax bill online possible?

Yes. The County Treasurer takes cards on its website with a 3% fee. Mail, phone, wire, counter, drop box and standing ACH debits are listed too.

Who decides what my Bay County house is worth for tax purposes?

Your township or city assessor makes that call. The county Equalization Department only tests whether assessments across units stay close to 49 to 50 percent.

How long do I have to take a homestead valuation to the Tax Tribunal?

For residential property the petition is due July 31 of the tax year, after the board of review protest. Commercial and industrial petitions are due May 31 under MCL 205.735a.

Must a Bay County deed carry a tax certificate?

Warranty deeds, land contracts and condominium master deeds do, and it costs $5 on a separate check to the County Treasurer. A quitclaim deed with no warranty is excused under MCL 211.135.

Where in Bad Axe do I take a Huron County property tax question?

Start in the county building at 250 East Huron Avenue, Bad Axe, MI 48413. The Treasurer sits in Room 204 (989-269-9238). Equalization is in Room 306 (989-269-6497), and Tax Mapping and GIS shares Room 306 (989-269-9421). Both offices post weekday hours from half past eight to half past four, with no lunch closure at the Treasurer's desk.

Valuation work happens nearer the house. In Michigan the assessing job belongs to each city or township, so whoever sets your value works for the unit that contains the house. The county home page links an Assessing and Tax Search page and a FetchGIS parcel map, and the Treasurer's page notes that the Huron County Land Bank runs out of the Treasurer's office.

Does my township or the county send the bill?

Your local collector sends the first bill. MCL 211.44 has the township treasurer or other collector mail a statement listing the parcel description, taxable value and tax due. Missing the mailing does not wipe out the tax. Anything unpaid as of March 1 is returned to the county treasurer, and the law has the collector note that return on the statement.

Huron County does some of the collecting itself. Its Treasurer takes ACH payments toward delinquent taxes and toward the summer taxes of the City of Harbor Beach and Grant Township. Fill in the authorization form and post it to PO Box 69, Bad Axe, MI 48413, or ring 989-269-9238 and finish the form by phone. Plastic is accepted too, at a 3 percent surcharge. Since the collecting office varies by unit, learn who holds your parcel's bill before you pay anyone.

What extra charges hit a tax bill that is paid late?

The charges step up with the calendar, and a local governing body can trim them. These come from MCL 211.44:

  • An administration fee of as much as 1 percent can be tacked on to a bill settled ahead of February 15 the next year.
  • After that, up to the delinquency date, the city or township may authorize a 3 percent late penalty.
  • Interest then builds at 1 percent monthly.
  • Any unpaid administration fee travels with the bill to the county treasurer.

The statute lets a governing body waive part of these charges for seniors, veterans and other listed groups. The office that mailed your bill can say whether you qualify.

Will the buyer pay more tax than I do?

Often, yes. Between sales, a parcel's taxable value may rise each year by no more than 5 percent or the inflation rate, whichever is lower, and never past state equalized value. A transfer of ownership ends the cap. MCL 211.27a sets the taxable value in the year after a transfer equal to state equalized value, a figure aimed at 50 percent of true cash value.

A conveyance by deed counts as a transfer. So a Huron County farmhouse owned for decades under a capped figure can carry a noticeably bigger bill in the first year for its new owner. Tell the buyer to budget for it.

When must a Huron County assessment appeal be filed?

A residential or farm owner goes to the local board of review first, then to the Michigan Tax Tribunal, with a petition due July 31 of that tax year. The July 31, 2026 date has therefore passed. Commercial and industrial owners have until May 31. The rules in MCL 205.735a set these dates.

Tribunal petition dates by type of dispute

Residential, agricultural or timber-cutover valueBoard of review, then TribunalJuly 31 that year
Commercial, industrial or developmental valueBoard of review, or Tribunal directlyMay 31 that year
Tax bill arithmetic mistakes onlyTribunalWithin 60 days of the mailing
Everything elseTribunalWithin 35 days of the final ruling

A fight over a principal residence exemption has to reach the July or December board of review before the Tribunal can take it. The local assessor knows when those boards sit.

What do the Census numbers show for Huron County homes?

Huron County fills the Thumb's northern tip, with 836 square miles of land, over 90 miles of coast and an economy built on farming. Its cities are Bad Axe, Caseville and Harbor Beach. Organization came in 1859 and the Bad Axe seat in 1873. Census Bureau figures sketch an older, settled market with modest prices:

  • A typical owner-occupied house is valued at $154,300, and owners live in 81.8 percent of all homes.
  • Households total 14,150, with median income of $58,870.
  • Monthly owner costs are $1,135 with a mortgage and $510 without, while median gross rent is $788.
  • Some 93.0 percent of residents stayed at one address for a year, and 29.7 percent are past 65.
  • Population dropped from 31,407 in 2020 to an estimated 30,530 in 2025.
  • Only 69 building permits were issued in 2025.
  • The median age at the 2020 census was 49.6 years.

Which local units bill Huron County owners?

Huron County has three cities, Bad Axe, Caseville and Harbor Beach, plus the unincorporated community of Bay Port and a ring of townships. Each unit assesses property inside its borders, and the first bill normally comes from the local collector. The county's part is to equalize values among the units, take in what goes delinquent and keep the parcel mapping. Grant Township is the one township the Treasurer's page names for summer tax payments, alongside the City of Harbor Beach, whose summer bills can be paid through the county office.

Parcels differ a great deal across the county. M-25 follows the shoreline of Saginaw Bay and Lake Huron, M-53 runs through the middle and M-19 serves the south. A lakefront cottage near Port Austin and a field near Bad Axe can sit in different units with different local levies. Ask the unit that mails your bill for its millage rate sheet.

What should I confirm about taxes before a Huron County closing?

Build a brief checklist and take it to the Treasurer and to your township or city office. Call 989-269-9238 and ask the parcel's standing, including delinquent sums sent to the county. Ask also whether the account has any open payment arrangement. Verify which unit collects each season's bill, since the county Treasurer handles summer taxes for Harbor Beach and Grant Township. For a warranty deed, ask whether a tax certificate is required at recording.

Keep each bill and receipt for the title company. If the Land Bank ever handled the parcel, ask what is of record. Value questions go to the assessor, and Equalization in Room 306 can name the right local unit.

More questions about Huron County, MI Property Tax Guide

Where can I pay overdue taxes in Huron County?

Walk them into Room 204 at 250 East Huron Avenue, or mail them to PO Box 69, Bad Axe, MI 48413. An ACH authorization form is available for delinquent taxes, and cards add a 3 percent fee.

When do unpaid taxes move to the Huron County treasurer?

On March 1. Taxes still open that day are handed to the county treasurer, according to MCL 211.44.

Does selling raise the next owner's bill in Huron County?

Usually. Under MCL 211.27a a transfer of ownership resets taxable value to state equalized value in the following year, which can be well above the capped figure on a home held for a long time.

What is the cutoff for taking an assessment to the Tax Tribunal?

July 31 for residential property, after a board of review protest, and the 2026 date is gone. Commercial and industrial parcels have until May 31.

Who can answer questions about my Huron County home's assessed value?

Your city or township assessor, since local units set assessments. The county Equalization Department at 989-269-6497 can point you to the right one.

Jackson County by the numbers

Whom do I pay for property tax in Jackson County, Michigan?

Start with your local city or township, which issues and collects the regular bill. The Jackson County Treasurer steps in only after a bill goes delinquent. A homeowner who is current writes the check to the local unit, while an owner who has slipped behind pays the county office instead.

The county spans roughly 702 square miles of land. Its only city is Jackson, the seat, and its villages are Brooklyn, Cement City (partly in the county), Concord, Grass Lake, Hanover, Parma and Springport. Townships cover the remainder. Each local unit bills its own residents, so before listing a house, confirm which unit sends yours.

What is the Jackson County property tax calendar?

All owners receive a summer bill in July and a winter bill in December. The table gives the recurring rules from the county's Current Tax Cycle page, and the City of Jackson follows its own schedule.

What happens when a Jackson County tax bill becomes delinquent?

Once a bill is delinquent it moves to the County Treasurer, and from then on payments go to that office alone. In the first delinquent month the charge is a 4 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest. After that, interest runs 1 percent monthly. Taxes left unpaid beyond a year carry a higher rate and extra fees.

The same office collects delinquent personal property tax for 18 units and runs the Delinquent Tax Revolving Fund, a pool that keeps cities, townships, villages, schools and the junior college whole while the county pursues what is owed. Each year it also holds a tax sale of real estate delinquent three or more years. An owner a few months behind has more choices than one approaching that third year, so act early.

How do I pay delinquent taxes to the Jackson County Treasurer?

The office sits on the first floor at 120 W. Michigan Avenue, Jackson, MI 49201, with the main line at 517-788-4418. It takes cash, checks, money orders and cards. Choose the route that suits your timing:

  • Phone (855) 246-9331, toll-free, with your parcel ID handy. Expect a 3 percent fee, minimum $2.00.
  • Online by credit card, with the same 3 percent fee.
  • Walk in to the office.
  • Mail a check made out to the Jackson County Treasurer, showing the parcel ID and which tax years it covers.

Ring 517-788-4418 for an exact payoff before you mail anything. A check the bank rejects returns the tax to the roll as unpaid, with every penalty and interest charge reinstated. Your city or township office can give you a missing parcel ID, and the county GIS parcel viewer can too.

Does a Jackson County deed need a tax certification?

For warranty deeds, yes. Certifying them is one of the Treasurer's listed duties, and state law requires the certification before such a deed is filed. Documents with a covenant of warranty follow the same path, so have your closing agent order it early.

Delinquent tax on the parcel means the closing runs through the Treasurer's payoff number, which you can request at 517-788-4418 ahead of closing day.

What should a Jackson County seller check before listing?

A few small checks head off most tax surprises at the closing table. Work through them in this order:

  • Find out whether your house is billed by the City of Jackson or by a township or village, since the payment calendars differ.
  • Look up the parcel on BS&A Online and read the delinquent tax search result for it.
  • If a prior year is unpaid, ask the Treasurer's Office for a payoff amount that includes penalty and interest through your expected closing date.
  • Ask your closing agent to order the treasurer's certification if the deed carries warranty language.
  • Confirm with the local assessor how the buyer will file the Property Transfer Affidavit.

City of Jackson owners have one extra wrinkle. Their summer bill can be paid in five monthly installments from July through November, so a house that sells in October may have some of the summer bill paid and some still open. Have the settlement statement show exactly which installments were paid.

Outside the city, the winter bill is where trouble starts, because February 14 passes quickly and the end of February is the cutoff for delinquency. A seller who closes in the spring should confirm the winter bill was paid in full.

Where can I check my Jackson County property record?

The county publishes records through BS&A Online. Searches work by address, name or parcel number, and the site offers assessing records, a property sale search, delinquent tax lookups and delinquent tax payments. A resident account may claim up to five properties for free.

Look at your assessing record before you list, since it shows what the local assessor holds on the house. If something looks off, take it to the city or township assessor, because assessing in Michigan is mostly a local job.

How big is the Jackson County housing market?

This is the largest of the four Michigan counties researched together here. QuickFacts estimates 159,552 residents and 69,801 housing units for 2025, with seniors making up 21.5 percent of the population. Owners occupy 75.0 percent of homes, with a midpoint value of $193,700 over 2020 to 2024. Rent at the midpoint reaches $985, the top of the four counties, against household income of $66,073. Permit counts reached 303 in 2025.

I-94 and US-127 both cross the county, along with M-50, M-52, M-60, M-99 and M-106, and workers average a 22.5 minute commute. The Grand River passes through the city of Jackson, and Waterloo State Recreation Area, about 21,000 acres, lies in the east.

How does selling change the next Jackson County tax bill?

Selling lifts the cap on taxable value. Michigan Treasury says the uncapping takes effect in the calendar year after the transfer of ownership, so a buyer can expect a bill closer to assessed value. The Property Transfer Affidavit, Form 2766, goes to the local assessor, and exempt transfers are catalogued in MCL 211.27a(7).

Summer and winter bills fall on different deadlines, so have your closing agent prorate current taxes on the settlement statement.

More questions about Jackson County, MI Property Tax Guide

When does a Jackson County property tax bill become delinquent?

Once February ends, whatever remains unpaid turns delinquent and moves to the County Treasurer. The first month adds a 4 percent penalty and 1 percent interest, and later months add 1 percent.

Is the Jackson County Treasurer where I pay my regular summer or winter bill?

No. You pay current bills to your city or township, and delinquent ones to the Treasurer. Inside the City of Jackson the summer bill is due by July 31, or in five installments.

How can I pay a delinquent tax by phone in Jackson County?

Call (855) 246-9331 and give your parcel ID. The phone fee is 3 percent with a $2.00 floor, and online card payments also carry 3 percent.

What if my Jackson County tax bill never arrives?

The county puts the burden on the owner to tell the local township or city that no bill came. Call that office promptly.

Does Jackson County sell homes for unpaid taxes?

Yes. The County Treasurer holds a yearly tax sale for real estate that has been delinquent three or more years. Call 517-788-4418 about your parcel well before that.

Lapeer County by the numbers

Which office bills me for property tax in Lapeer County?

Your township, city or village treasurer sends it, and the county treasurer only gets involved when a bill goes unpaid. The summer bill is dated July 1 and the winter bill December 1, and whatever remains open after March 1 is handed to the Lapeer County Treasurer as delinquent.

The county covers 663 square miles, of which 643 are land, in the part of Michigan known as the Thumb. The City of Lapeer serves as county seat, with Imlay City and Brown City as the other two cities. The villages are Almont, Clifford, Columbiaville, Dryden, Metamora, North Branch and Otter Lake. Eighteen townships fill in the rest. Because each unit runs its own treasurer and assessor, the first call about a bill always goes to the office for the place where the house sits.

  • Questions about a current bill: the local treasurer. The county treasurer cannot waive local penalties or interest.
  • Value, classification or a principal residence claim: the local assessor.
  • Taxes that turned delinquent after March 1: the County Treasurer in the County Complex at 255 Clay Street, Lapeer.
  • Getting a prior owner's name off a bill: the local assessor, with a deed or other proof of the transfer.

What does the Lapeer County equalization office do?

It checks that assessments are fair between local units, and it does not set the assessment on any one house. The department advises the Board of Commissioners on true cash value and runs annual sales and appraisal studies for each class of property.

That work rests on section 211.34 of the General Property Tax Act, which tells the county board to review each township and city roll for uniformity every year. If your own assessed value looks wrong, take it to the local assessor first. The county office exists to correct gaps between units, such as one township running below the sales level of its neighbors. Public hearings on county operating millage are held in the Commission Chambers at the County Complex, and a notice for a proposed 0.4881 mill increase on 2024 levies shows how those hearings are announced.

How expensive is a missed due date in Lapeer County?

A late bill picks up a flat administration fee and monthly interest, and the county treasurer has no power to waive them. The schedule below comes from the Lapeer County Treasurer's published FAQ.

ChargeAmountWhen it applies
Administration fee4%Added March 1, when unpaid taxes turn delinquent
Interest, first delinquent year1% per monthCounted back to the date the bill was first due
Interest after forfeiture1.5% per monthStarts the following March 1 and reaches back to the turnover date
Title search fee$175Added at forfeiture
Recording fees$60Added at forfeiture

Source: Lapeer County Treasurer FAQ, citing MCL 211.56 and 211.78.

The office takes personal checks, cashier's checks, money orders, credit cards and cash, with checks payable to Lapeer County Treasurer. Partial payments may be sent whenever you like, and a receipt comes back to the return address. Fees and interest keep running on whatever balance remains.

Mortgage servicers sometimes miss a payment. The treasurer's FAQ states that the owner, not the lender, carries the responsibility, so compare each mortgage statement with the local treasurer's records.

How does tax foreclosure work in Lapeer County?

Foreclosure can begin once taxes are two years delinquent, and the county treasurer then sells the property at public auction. A 1999 law, Public Act 123 (MCL 211.78), cut the time owners have to catch up on unpaid bills.

Forfeiture falls on March 1, one year after the turnover date, and it only prepares the parcel for foreclosure. The treasurer's page states plainly that the property is not lost at forfeiture. The later foreclosure is final, and nothing returns the house to the owner afterward.

  • State law requires five notices: two by first class mail, two by certified mail and one by personal service. The county sends another three to five on its own.
  • Names and addresses of delinquent owners are published in the newspaper, and recorded lienholders, mortgage holders and land contract holders are notified.
  • At the first auction the minimum bid equals all taxes, interest and fees. If a parcel does not sell, a very low minimum applies at the second auction.
  • The foreclosure list is normally available around May 1 each year. Mortgage foreclosures are not run by this office.

Anyone behind on taxes who wants to sell should do it before forfeiture, because the $175 and $60 charges and the higher interest rate arrive on that date.

What if my Lapeer County assessment looks too high?

Begin at the March board of review in the township, city or village where the house stands. Each unit sets its own meeting dates, so call the local assessor.

For residential property the board of review comes first. Under MCL 205.735a, you then petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal no later than July 31 of the assessment year. Commercial and industrial real property can go straight to the Tribunal, with a May 31 filing date. A petition over an arithmetic error on a bill has its own 60 day limit. Owners representing themselves are allowed to appear without an attorney.

Which exemptions can lower a Lapeer County tax bill?

The principal residence exemption is the main one for homeowners. It lifts the school district operating levy, up to 18 mills, from a residence that a Michigan resident owns and lives in.

  • Form 2368 goes to the local assessor. The county FAQ names two dates: June 1 ahead of summer billing and November 1 ahead of winter billing.
  • A denied claim can go to an informal conference with the Department of Treasury's exemption unit, or to the Tax Tribunal.
  • The poverty exemption is requested at the city or township assessor's office.
  • The county treasurer also accepts financial hardship deferral applications. Ask that office what documents it wants.

The principal residence exemption is separate from the Homestead Property Tax Credit, which is filed with the Michigan income tax return.

What does a Lapeer County seller owe at closing?

Transfer tax is the seller's cost, collected when the deed is recorded. At the county's published rates, a $200,000 price produces $220 for the county and $1,500 for the state, $1,720 in all.

A deed with a covenant of warranty, or a land contract, also needs the County Treasurer's $5 certification under MCL 211.135, and recording adds $30. How the current year's bill is prorated depends on the purchase agreement and the settlement statement prepared by the title company. If an earlier year is delinquent, request a payoff figure from the County Treasurer before closing so the interest and fees are counted correctly.

More questions about Lapeer County, MI Property Tax Guide

On what date do Lapeer County property taxes go delinquent?

Unpaid summer and winter bills turn delinquent after March 1 and move to the Lapeer County Treasurer. That is also the day the 4% administration fee is added and 1% monthly interest is counted from the original due date.

Can the Lapeer County treasurer waive penalties?

No. The treasurer's FAQ says the fees and interest in the property tax act have no waiver provision, and the office cannot remove them. Ask about the financial hardship deferral if a one-time expense caused the delay.

May I pay a late Lapeer County bill in installments?

Yes. Send any amount at any time, and a receipt comes back by mail. Statutory fees and interest still apply to whatever is left unpaid.

How long before Lapeer County can foreclose on unpaid taxes?

Two years from the delinquency. Forfeiture comes a year after turnover on March 1, and foreclosure follows after the notices are served. Foreclosed parcels go to public auction.

Who removes my name from the bill after a sale?

The local assessor in the township, city or village where the house is. The county treasurer has no authority to change a name on a bill, so bring the deed or proof of transfer to the assessor.

Who collects property tax in Lenawee County?

Your local city, village or township treasurer collects the current bill, and the Lenawee County Treasurer takes over once a bill is delinquent. On March 1 each year the county treasurer receives all delinquent taxes from the townships and cities through a step called settlement, and the local units are made whole from the county's Delinquent Tax Fund.

The county treasurer does not collect winter taxes for the current year until they turn delinquent on March 1. Your local treasurer takes payments through the end of February. The county office is on North Main Street in Adrian (mailing address 301 N. Main Street, Adrian, MI 49221), reachable at 517-264-4554, and it is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to noon and 1:00 p.m. to 4:30 p.m.

  • Value and taxable value questions start with the assessor, and the county Equalization Department answers at 517-264-4522 on the first floor of the Old Courthouse.

What does Lenawee County look like for a property owner?

Lenawee County is in southeast Michigan along the Ohio line, with Adrian as the county seat and largest city. It covers 761 square miles, 750 of them land, and borders Jackson, Washtenaw, Monroe and Hillsdale counties in Michigan plus Lucas and Fulton counties in Ohio. The county was created in 1822 from Monroe County and organized in 1826.

The 2020 census counted 99,423 residents, with a 2025 estimate of 97,779. That census found 43,577 housing units, 11.5% of them vacant, and 77.3% of occupied homes were owner occupied. Housing stock ranges from city lots in Adrian, Tecumseh, Hudson and Morenci to lake homes in the Manitou Beach and Devils Lake area and rural parcels spread across the townships. Fourteen school districts serve the county, including Adrian City, Tecumseh Public Schools, Onsted Community Schools and Blissfield Community Schools. Adrian College and Siena Heights University are both in Adrian.

Besides Adrian, the county has villages at Addison, Blissfield, Britton, Clayton, Clinton, Deerfield and Onsted, plus part of Cement City, and the townships run from Blissfield and Cambridge to Seneca, Tecumseh and Woodstock. Parcel numbers carry a code for the taxing unit. In the 2026 sale notice, keys starting XA0 belong to the City of Adrian, MD0 to Madison Township and FAW to Weston Village, so the first letters of a parcel number tell you which local office issues the bill.

How do I pay a Lenawee County property tax bill?

You can pay online through the county's BS&A portal, or in person, by mail or by phone for delinquent bills. The county's assessment page walks through the online steps.

  • Open the county's online service and choose Property and Land Search.
  • Search by parcel number, address or owner name in "Smith, John" form.
  • Register an account, confirm the parcel from the email, then log back in and select Pay My Taxes.
  • At the counter, the treasurer accepts cash, check, cashier's check, money order and credit or debit cards. Cards carry an enhanced access fee.

Homeowners who cannot manage the summer bill can ask about the State of Michigan's summer tax deferment. The treasurer's FAQ links to both the state's requirements and its application.

The notice also said buyers inherit the 2026 winter taxes, and that deeds are prepared in the name on the IRS W-9. Watch the treasurer's news page for the next sale notice, because bidders must register on the auction site before the sale opens.

How do I appeal a Lenawee County assessment?

Take it to the local board of review in March, then, for a home, to the Michigan Tax Tribunal by July 31. The assessor in your city or township can tell you the board's meeting dates.

The county's assessment page lists the questions owners ask most, such as why an assessment changed when nothing was done to the property, what happens to taxable value after a purchase and how assessed value, state equalized value and taxable value differ. MCL 205.735a sets July 31 for residential and agricultural property and May 31 for commercial and industrial. Other determinations carry a 35 day window from the final decision. For a home, the March board of review must hear the protest first, so a missed March meeting usually ends the appeal for that year.

How does the Lenawee County Treasurer certify taxes on a sale or land split?

The treasurer certifies that taxes are paid in full for the past five years, as MCL 211.135 allows. That certificate is needed on deeds, land contracts and property splits.

  • The office compares the deed's legal description with the Equalization Department's electronic records. A mismatch stops certification until the Equalization Department or local assessor approves the description.
  • For a deed made from a combined or divided parcel, the "parent" parcel's taxes are checked too.
  • For a land split, ask the local assessor whether a split is allowed, then bring the Land Split Certification Form and $5.00 to the treasurer. The fee is kept whether the certification is approved or denied.
  • A split is denied if taxes are delinquent. Public Act 23 of 2019 put this duty on county treasurers.

What should a Lenawee County seller do about taxes?

Check the parcel number on your deed against the county's online record, then confirm with the treasurer that nothing is delinquent. A clean certificate keeps the deed moving at closing. If a balance exists, ask the treasurer for a payoff figure so it can be settled from the sale.

Condition has no effect on any of this. A house with deferred repairs or tenants in place still needs the same certificate, because the record belongs to the parcel number and legal description on file with the Equalization Department. If the legal description on your deed differs from the county's, resolve that with the assessor before the closing date, since the treasurer will not certify a deed that does not match.

When do Lenawee County taxes go to the county treasurer?

On March 1. Unpaid bills from the townships and cities pass to the county through settlement that day. Before then, current winter taxes are paid to your local treasurer through the end of February.

Does the Lenawee County treasurer accept credit cards?

Yes, along with cash, checks, cashier's checks and money orders. Card payments carry an enhanced access fee. Delinquent bills can also be paid by phone through the county's BS&A system.

Where is the Lenawee County treasurer's office?

At 301 N. Main Street in Adrian. Hours are 8:00 a.m. to noon and 1:00 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, and the office closes for lunch between noon and 1:00 p.m.

Five years of taxes. The treasurer confirms that all taxes on the parcel are paid for that period, using the parcel number and legal description on the deed.

No. Bidding ran from August 11, 2026, with payment due by noon on August 13. Ask the county treasurer about any parcels offered later.

Livingston County by the numbers

Who handles property tax in Livingston County, Michigan?

Three layers share the work. Each city or township assessor sets the value of a parcel. The county Equalization Department checks those assessments for uniformity and reports equalized values. The local city or township treasurer bills the current summer and winter taxes, and the Livingston County Treasurer takes over collection once taxes turn delinquent.

That split matters when you call. The county treasurer's own FAQ says the current summer or winter amount is available from your local city or township treasurer, and a bill question for a house in Howell goes to a different office than one in Genoa Township. The county treasurer's page also lists tax clearance of deeds among its duties and charges $2.50 to view a parcel's tax history online, a fee that is not available by phone request.

  • County Treasurer: (517) 546-7010, weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., at 200 E Grand River Ave, Howell.
  • Equalization Department: (517) 546-4182, weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., at 304 E Grand River Ave, Howell.
  • Current bill, due dates and payment: your city or township treasurer.
  • Valuation or exemption question: your city or township assessor.

Livingston County has 585 square miles of area, a 2020 population of 193,866 and 78,441 housing units, of which 5.3 percent were vacant. Howell is the county seat, and most commuters head toward Detroit, Lansing, Ann Arbor or Flint on I-96, US 23 and M-59.

How is a Livingston County home's taxable value calculated?

Each bill starts from taxable value, a figure that can sit far below what the house would sell for. The county Equalization Department publishes a short glossary of how the numbers connect, and it explains why two neighbors with identical houses can pay very different bills.

Value terms used by the Livingston County Equalization Department
TermMeaning
Assessed value50 percent of the usual selling price, or true cash value
State equalized valueAssessed value after county and state equalization; usually equal to assessed value
Capped valueLast year's taxable value, less losses, raised by inflation or 5 percent (whichever is less), plus additions
Taxable valueThe lesser of state equalized value or capped value

Losses are parts of a property physically removed, such as a garage. Additions are parts physically added, such as a finished basement or a new family room. A home owner who has held a property for many years usually has a taxable value well below the state equalized value, because the cap grows more slowly than market prices.

What happens to the tax bill after a Livingston County sale?

The cap lifts. In the year following a transfer of ownership, taxable value is uncapped and equals the state equalized value. The capped formula resumes the next year and runs until the next transfer. A buyer who sees the seller's old tax bill should not assume it will stay that low.

The buyer must file a property transfer affidavit with the assessor in the city or township where the home sits within 45 days. Failing to file can bring a fine of $5 a day, up to $200. Sellers who want a smooth closing can remind the buyer's agent of this step, since the affidavit also tells the assessor who should receive the next bill.

  • Seller's side: tax history from the county treasurer, a payoff of any delinquent balance, and the title company's tax proration.
  • Buyer's side: the transfer affidavit, a request for the principal residence exemption if the home will be a primary residence, and an estimate of the uncapped bill.
  • Both: confirm whether special assessments are attached to the parcel.

How do Livingston County owners appeal an assessment?

Michigan appeals begin locally. If you believe the assessor has valued your home above half of its true cash value, you take the question to the city or township Board of Review in March, then to the Michigan Tax Tribunal if you are still unsatisfied. Individual appeals are heard at that local level. The county Equalization Department can supply Board of Review information, appraisal study results, assessment roll data, equalized values and taxable values on request.

For parcel-level data, call (517) 546-4182 or email equalization@livgov.com to get an order number. The office is at 304 E Grand River Ave in Howell and is open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. except county holidays. Bulk digital exports are priced at $0.04 per parcel, with a small per-sort addition for custom exports.

Equalization also keeps top-ten taxpayer information and State Tax Commission forms. The annual equalization and apportionment reports are posted on the county site for each year, which helps a seller compare how neighboring townships were treated.

What if taxes on a Livingston County house go unpaid?

The county treasurer is the collector of all delinquent real property taxes. Michigan's process runs three years. A parcel is forfeited to the county treasurer when its real property taxes are in the second year of delinquency, and taxes still unpaid on March 31 of the third year are foreclosed by the county as foreclosing governmental unit. People with an interest in the property at the time may claim excess proceeds from a sale, within statutory deadlines.

The practical advice for a seller is to ask the Livingston County Treasurer for a written payoff before listing, because interest and fees grow the longer a balance sits. Most closings clear the balance from the proceeds.

Many owners with back taxes also have a mortgage in arrears or an inherited house they cannot keep up. Selling for cash can end the problem before the forfeiture year, and the purchase price covers the payoff at closing.

Which Livingston County exemptions can lower a bill?

The Equalization Department lists two: the homeowner's principal residence percentage, which is the part of a home you own and occupy that is exempt from certain school taxes, and the qualified agricultural exemption for property used mainly for farming. A new owner should ask the local assessor how and by when to claim the principal residence exemption for the home.

Michigan's constitution, quoted on the Equalization page, requires uniform assessment of property and caps assessed value at 50 percent of true cash value, which is why the local numbers on a bill look lower than a sale price. A buyer comparing a Livingston County listing with a similar one in another state should start from taxable value when estimating the yearly bill.

Other relief, such as hardship or poverty exemptions, is handled by the local assessing unit, and an owner should ask that office before the March Board of Review window. The Wayne County Treasurer, in a neighboring county, gives the same direction for the poverty exemption: reach out to your local assessing unit.

More questions about Livingston County, MI Property Tax Guide

Who sends the Livingston County property tax bill?

Your city or township treasurer does. The county treasurer collects only after taxes turn delinquent, and its FAQ tells owners to ask the local treasurer for current summer and winter amounts.

How is taxable value different from state equalized value in Livingston County?

Taxable value is the lesser of state equalized value and capped value. The cap limits yearly growth to inflation or 5 percent, whichever is lower, until the property transfers.

Does my Livingston County tax bill go up when I buy a house?

It can. Taxable value is uncapped in the year after a transfer and equals state equalized value, then the cap resumes. File the property transfer affidavit within 45 days.

Where do I appeal my Livingston County assessment?

Start with the Board of Review in your city or township in March. If that does not resolve it, the Michigan Tax Tribunal is the next step. The county Equalization Department can provide supporting data.

How long before Livingston County can foreclose for unpaid taxes?

Michigan's process spans three years. Parcels forfeit in the second year of delinquency, and unpaid real property taxes at March 31 of the third year are foreclosed.

Delinquent real or personal property tax can be paid online with a debit card or ACH, and a GIS search returns legal descriptions from an address or tax ID.

Who can change a Macomb County assessment?

Start with the local board of review, because the county cannot do it. The Macomb County Equalization Department (586-469-5260, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.) runs sales and appraisal studies by property class in each city and township to check that local assessments are fair across the county, and it states that it does not determine an individual property's assessment. Its authority is Section 211.34 of the General Property Tax Act.

A protest starts at the board of review, whose first March meeting falls on the second Monday, or the Tuesday or Wednesday after if the local government chose that. Under MCL 211.30 it must hold at least 12 hours of hearings that week, including three hours after 6 p.m. Nonresidents may protest by letter, and local governments may extend that option to residents.

The written decision arrives by the first Monday in June and points to the Michigan Tax Tribunal as the next step, with a filing date printed on the notice. Keep that notice. If you miss the March session, the next opening is the following March.

Will a sale raise the next tax bill on a Macomb County house?

Usually yes. A long-held home carries a taxable value held down by an annual cap, and a sale lifts that value to the state equalized value, which tracks about half the market price, for the next year. The mechanics are in MCL 211.27a. The buyer, not the seller, files the change notice with the assessor, and has 45 days to do it.

Not every transfer counts as a sale for this purpose. The statute exempts:

  • Moves between spouses.
  • Residential transfers to a parent, child, sibling or grandchild that stay non-commercial.
  • Foreclosure transfers, until the lender resells.
  • Court-ordered transfers with no stated price.

For a seller, this means the buyer's carrying cost can differ sharply from yours, and a seller who owned for decades may want to tell a buyer to expect a higher bill. The assessor in your own city or township can quote the current taxable value, and the county Treasurer's tax histories show what has been paid. Sellers handling an estate should check whether the heir is a close relative under the statute, since that decides whether the taxable value resets when title moves out of the decedent's name.

What does the county charge once taxes go delinquent?

On March 1 following the tax year, unpaid real property tax becomes payable to the County Treasurer, with a 4% administration fee and interest at 1% per month. The fee is spelled out in the county's delinquent tax FAQ, which also warns that forfeiture a year later raises the rate to 1.5% per month, applied back to the original delinquency date.

The county describes the sequence as a three-year forfeiture and foreclosure process. The published schedule for 2025 taxes shows how the notices and fees stack up:

Macomb County Treasurer schedule for unpaid 2025 property taxes
DateWhat happens
March 3, 2026Taxes delinquent, 4% fee and 1% interest added
June 1 and September 1, 2026First class mail notices
October 1, 2026$15 fee added
March 1, 2027Forfeiture, $175 minimum title search fee
September 1, 2027Personal visit, $50 fee
January 2028Show cause hearing with the Treasurer
March 31, 2028Foreclosure final, redemption ends

A circuit court hearing in February 2028 produces the foreclosure judgment, and a $35 publication fee is added in November 2027.

How many warnings does a Macomb County owner get before foreclosure?

The county FAQ lists what an owner should receive before foreclosure:

  • Four first class mail notices.
  • Two certified mail notices.
  • Three notices published in a county newspaper.
  • Staff visits to the property beginning each September, repeated until the redemption period expires.

The Treasurer's Office also offers to explain the process, set up a payment plan or point owners to assistance programs through its tax foreclosure prevention page.

Once foreclosure is final, the owner cannot get the property back. It is offered first to the State of Michigan at fair market value, then to the local community, and what remains goes to public auction held between the third Tuesday in July and the first Tuesday in November, with notice published 30 days ahead.

Money left over after an auction can belong to the former owner. For auctions beginning in 2021, anyone who held an interest at the time of foreclosure may file a claim for proceeds above the taxes owed. The county is also taking part in a settlement of claims for surplus proceeds from auctions before 2021, listed on the Treasurer's page as the Fox class action. In the 2025 tax year timeline, the claim deadline is July 1, 2028.

How are back taxes dealt with when selling a Macomb County home?

Request a payoff figure from the Treasurer that runs through the planned closing date, and let the title company settle it out of the seller's proceeds. Interest at 1% per month keeps growing in the first year, so a payoff quoted for the first of a month changes the next month.

The register of deeds will record a warranty deed only with a Treasurer's certificate showing no unpaid tax for the preceding five years, under MCL 211.135. A seller who is still in the first delinquent year has the most room to act, because forfeiture fees such as the $175 title search charge have not yet been added.

Michigan also allows a collecting unit to add up to a 1% administration fee on bills paid before February 15 and a 3% late penalty from February 15 until the bill is returned as delinquent, if the municipality has authorized it. Ask your own city or township treasurer what it charges.

More questions about Macomb County, MI Property Tax Guide

When does Macomb County treat property tax as delinquent?

March 1 of the year after the tax year. For 2025 taxes the county's published date is March 3, 2026, when a 4% fee and 1% interest are added.

Who sets my Macomb County property assessment?

Your city or township assessor does. The county Equalization Department at 586-469-5260 compares assessments across the county and says it does not determine any individual property's assessment.

How long until Macomb County forecloses on unpaid property tax?

About three years. Property is forfeited after the first year, and unpaid taxes as of March 31 in the third year of delinquency lead to foreclosure and title passing to the county treasurer.

Does selling change my Macomb County taxable value?

The seller's value does not carry over to the buyer. After a transfer of ownership, the next year's taxable value is set at the state equalized value, and the buyer reports the transfer to the assessor within 45 days.

Can I recover auction proceeds after a Macomb County tax foreclosure?

Possibly. Former owners and others with an interest can file to claim proceeds above the taxes owed, under the county's published deadlines, and a separate class action settlement covers auctions before 2021.

Mecosta County by the numbers

Which offices handle property tax in Mecosta County?

Property tax here passes through four desks, and each answers a separate question. The local assessor puts a value on the house. The township or city treasurer mails the first bill and takes the first payment. Equalization at the county tests whether each unit values property evenly. The county treasurer inherits whatever is still unpaid on March 1.

The Equalization Department, reachable at (231) 592-0108, does not set an individual owner's assessment. It studies whole property classes in the county's 16 townships and one city so the Board of Commissioners can equalize each class to 50 percent of true cash value. Its page also carries the annual millage rates, the apportionment report, a property tax estimator and a list of township assessors.

The county treasurer's page sends owners to Equalization at the same number for name and address changes. Owners in a village receive two bills in July, one from the township and one from the village, and each is paid to its own treasurer.

What are the Mecosta County property tax due dates?

Bills for the summer levy are mailed in the first week of July and can be paid without penalty through September 14. The winter bill follows in December. The county treasurer's page quotes MCL 211.44(2): a bill that is lost or never received does not cancel the tax, so ask the township, city or village if nothing arrives.

What happens if property taxes go unpaid in Mecosta County?

The path runs through forfeiture to foreclosure. Roughly 23 months of delinquency ends in foreclosure, with title moving to the State of Michigan, because the state serves as Mecosta County's foreclosing governmental unit. The state auctions the parcel, and the sale results appear on Tax-Sale.info.

When an auction brings in more than what was owed, the former owner may claim the surplus. The county treasurer's page walks through the steps: file Form 5743 with the state by the July 1 after the foreclosure date, wait for the state's response, then ask the circuit court for payment between February 1 and May 15. The separate window for pre-2021 sales closed March 31, 2025.

For anyone a few months behind, March 1 is the date to beat. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure and, if you plan to sell, close before the parcel hits forfeiture.

How does a sale change the taxes on a Mecosta County house?

A sale usually raises the taxable value. Year over year, taxable value may rise by no more than 5 percent or the inflation rate, whichever is less, but a change of ownership removes that limit and sets taxable value equal to the state equalized value the next year (MCL 211.27a). A long-time owner's bill can therefore look quite different on the buyer's first statement.

Some changes of hands leave the cap alone, among them transfers between spouses, certain residential transfers to a parent, child, sibling or grandchild who will not use the property commercially, and a foreclosure until the lender resells. The new owner has 45 days to tell the assessor, and the Property Transfer Affidavit is on the county's Equalization forms page as Form 2766.

Sellers who claimed the principal residence exemption should withdraw it after they move. The same page offers Form 2602 for that request and Form 2368 for the buyer's homestead affidavit. Farmland owners will also find the farmland exemption claim (Form 2599) and the qualified agricultural property affidavit (Form 3676) there.

How do I appeal a Mecosta County assessment?

Begin at the Board of Review in your township or city, which meets the week of the second Monday in March (MCL 211.30). The week must include at least 12 hours of sessions, some after 6 p.m. You may protest in person, send an agent, or write a letter where the local unit has allowed that.

The board owes written notice of its decision by the first Monday in June. An owner who still disagrees can petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal: July 31 of the tax year for residential and agricultural property, May 31 for commercial and industrial (MCL 205.735a). A residential owner generally must have protested to the Board of Review first.

Questions about one assessment go to the township hall, and the Equalization page keeps a list of township assessors. Four townships publish hall details on the county's township page:

  • Colfax, hall at 14428 157th Ave., meets the third Wednesday at 6 p.m.
  • Grant, hall at 14982 21 Mile Rd., meets the second Monday at 6:30 p.m.
  • Hinton, hall at 9013 3 Mile Rd., Lakeview, meets the second Monday at 7 p.m.
  • Millbrook, hall at 3015 Jackson Rd., Blanchard, meets the first Monday at 7 p.m. and keeps office hours by appointment

The villages of Mecosta and Stanwood meet the first Monday at 6 p.m. and the second Monday at 7 p.m. respectively. The rest of the townships maintain their own websites.

What do Mecosta County property taxes mean for a seller at closing?

Closing usually includes a proration of the current bill, and for a warranty deed the county treasurer must certify that five years of taxes are paid (MCL 211.135). Afterward the register of deeds in Big Rapids records the deed and the assessors learn of the transfer.

The federal survey for 2020 to 2024 reports a typical house value of $178,900, monthly owner costs of $1,293 with a mortgage and $480 without, and household income near $60,951. Those numbers hint at what a buyer can carry, though the real bill turns on the township, village and school district millage on each parcel.

  • Ask the township or city treasurer for the current balance, and the county treasurer for any delinquent amount.
  • Find the parcel's millage in the county's published millage rates for the year.
  • Rescind any principal residence exemption after the sale.
  • Give the buyer the date by which the transfer affidavit is due.

More questions about Mecosta County, MI Property Tax Guide

What is the deadline for the summer tax bill in Mecosta County?

September 14 is the last penalty-free day. Winter bills follow in December, and after February 14 townships may add 3 percent through the end of that month. March 1 sends anything unpaid to the county treasurer.

What does a late Mecosta County bill cost?

Interest of 1 percent a month starts after September 14 on the summer bill. At the county treasurer, a 4 percent administration charge is added, and interest climbs to 1.5 percent a month after forfeiture.

When does Mecosta County property reach tax foreclosure?

After roughly 23 months of delinquency. Forfeiture comes after the first year, and the State of Michigan then auctions the foreclosed parcel.

Does the county or my township decide what my Mecosta County house is worth?

The township or city assessor decides it. Equalization at the county measures whether each unit assesses at 50 percent of true cash value but does not value individual homes.

Is there a way to recover surplus from a Mecosta County tax sale?

Yes, when the auction price exceeds the debt. File Form 5743 by July 1 after the foreclosure date, then make a circuit court motion between February 1 and May 15.

Which Oakland County offices handle property tax?

For the fourteen units the county assesses, Equalization keeps separate lines: 248-858-8793 for property transfers and homestead claims, and 248-858-0776 for appraisal records and tax descriptions. Use them if you sold or bought recently and the bill still shows the earlier owner.

Equalization works across 52 assessing jurisdictions, adjusting each class of property so they all reach a common level of valuation. The division also decides homestead exemption questions, reassesses ownership transfers and reviews millage rollback calculations. For fourteen units, including Novi Township, Lyon Township, South Lyon, Pontiac and Rochester, it acts as the assessor itself and takes all assessment questions.

What does Oakland County look like for a home seller?

Oakland County is a large Metro Detroit county with 867 square miles of land and 1,288,337 residents in the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate. Pontiac is where the county's tax and records offices sit. Housing is mostly owner-occupied, at 72.7%, and the median owner-occupied home was valued at $343,600 for 2020 to 2024.

Median household income runs $97,760, and median gross rent is $1,376. The county counted 569,537 housing units in 2025 and issued 2,023 building permits that year.

Because the county is so large, ask the local assessor which school and special districts apply to your parcel, since the millage total depends on them.

How are Oakland County taxes calculated and appealed?

A bill equals taxable value divided by 1,000 and multiplied by the millage total for the parcel's taxing units. Assessed value is about half of market value, and taxable value is capped at the lesser of assessed value or the prior year's taxable value times the inflation multiplier, with a 5% ceiling. A change of ownership removes the cap for the following year.

Valuation appeals begin at the local March Board of Review. Michigan law gives owners one chance a year to challenge a residential value there, and the Michigan Tax Tribunal is the next step, with residential petitions due July 31 after a March appearance. File the petition with the board of review for your city or township.

Relief programs sit mostly with the local unit. Cities such as Novi publish a poverty exemption application and a summer tax deferral process, and the county treasurer offers repayment help once a balance is delinquent.

How do you pay Oakland County property tax online?

Oakland County runs a countywide payment portal through PayIt for current bills, delinquent balances and personal property tax. You search by street address or parcel number, then pay as a guest or with an account. The portal lets you pay current taxes on several parcels in the same city, village or township in one visit.

  • eCheck or ACH payments carry a $2.50 fee.

Payment history in the portal starts with payments made on or after July 1, 2025. A payment made against the wrong tax year is not transferable, so read the Available Bills list before you check out.

What happens when property taxes go unpaid in Oakland County?

Is there help for Oakland County owners behind on tax?

The office posts a financial assistance page and a foreclosure prevention page, and contractors visit delinquent parcels to hand over information. Do not wait for the final notice, because fees and the 18% interest on forfeited parcels keep adding up each month.

Former owners can also claim surplus when a foreclosed parcel sells for more than the debt. The county's timeline has claimants file by July 1, learn of any proceeds the following January, file with the court between February and May, and receive payment within 21 days of the court's order.

How do you sell an Oakland County house with tax due?

Order an official delinquent tax statement before you list. Title companies, owners and others can buy one through the county's Property Gateway system, and it shows what the county treasurer holds against the parcel. The local treasurer will give you the current-year balance separately.

At the Register of Deeds, a warranty deed or any deed with a warranty clause needs a tax certification from the county treasurer, which costs $5. That certification confirms taxes are up to date. If back taxes are owed, the title company pays them from the seller's proceeds so the certification can issue and the deed can be recorded. See the county's Register of Deeds guide for recording costs.

Pay your city, village or township treasurer. The county treasurer takes payment once a bill has become delinquent, and its portal can handle both kinds in the same system.

March 31, 2027. The Oakland County Treasurer's notices set that date as the last day to pay unpaid 2024 and earlier taxes and keep the property. Foreclosure takes effect April 1.

Three layers touch each tax bill in this county. How are Saginaw County properties valued, and how do owners appeal?

Michigan sets assessments at half of true cash value. The figure that gets multiplied by the millage, taxable value, climbs by the smaller of 5% or the inflation rate each year until a sale resets it (MCL 211.27a). Your assessment notice shows both numbers.

Each local board of review opens on the second Monday of March and must sit at least 12 hours during that week, with evening time included (MCL 211.30). A township or city can also allow protests by letter, and a nonresident owner can file by letter regardless.

The City of Saginaw notes that July and December boards sit only when there are errors to correct or poverty exemptions to weigh, and that every board can rule on poverty exemption applications for the current year. Each local unit sets its own schedule, so check with your assessor before assuming a date.

What happens when Saginaw County taxes go delinquent?

Past-due real property tax is payable at the counter, by mail or on the web. Counter payments can be cash, money order or certified check, while personal checks work only for first-year delinquencies before January 1. Visa, MasterCard and Discover are taken, and the mailing address is Saginaw County Treasurer, 111 S. Michigan Avenue, Saginaw, MI 48602.

The web option runs at all hours through a vendor, which charges an access fee on the whole payment. The card policy contains these rules:

  • A photo ID issued by a government must accompany a card payment, and the card must carry the payer's name.
  • If a payment is reversed or declined, it is treated as void and all fees, interest and forfeiture fees reapply from the original date.
  • A voided payment that had a redemption certificate recorded adds $20 for the correction.
  • An overpayment below $3 is absorbed into interest, and larger refunds return to the same card.
  • Payments post to the parcel you name, with no refund for paying the wrong parcel.

The county was also a defendant in Fox v. Saginaw County, a federal class action settled over surplus money from tax foreclosure auctions between 2013 and 2020. Claims closed on July 16, 2026.

Does selling reset the tax bill in Saginaw County?

Yes. The year after a sale, taxable value jumps to state equalized value, and the buyer has 45 days to report the transfer to the local assessor on a state form. Some transfers do not count as a change of ownership, including a transfer between spouses, a residential transfer to a close relative such as a parent, child or grandchild with no commercial use afterward, and certain trust and foreclosure transfers.

A warranty deed arriving at the register also needs the Treasurer's certificate, priced at $5 for the first five descriptions and $1 per extra description. State law ties it to proof that the preceding five years of taxes are paid (MCL 211.135). Quitclaim deeds without a warranty are excepted. Request a written payoff from the Treasurer before choosing a closing date if any year is delinquent.

How big is the Saginaw County housing stock?

Saginaw County covers 816 square miles in Mid-Michigan, drained by rivers that join into the Saginaw River. The 2020 census recorded 190,124 residents in 78,442 households and 85,953 housing units, 8.7% of them empty. Owners held 70.5% of occupied homes. Single-person households made up roughly a third of the total, and the median age was 41.3.

The cities are Saginaw, Frankenmuth and Zilwaukee, and the rest is townships such as Birch Run, Chesaning, Kochville and Swan Creek. I-75 and I-675 serve the metro area, and US 23 plus M-13, M-46 and M-47 fill in the grid. MBS International Airport sits near Freeland.

A parcel's school district changes the bill. Districts include Saginaw Public Schools, Saginaw Township Community Schools, Frankenmuth, Chesaning Union, Birch Run Area, Freeland Community, Hemlock Public, Swan Valley and Bridgeport-Spaulding. Saginaw Valley State University and Delta College anchor higher education.

How old is the Saginaw County tax base?

The county was created by September 10, 1822 and fully organized on February 9, 1835. Sawmills and farms were spreading along the river by the early 1850s, and the Michigan historical markers in the county include the Saginaw Valley lumbering era, Saginaw oil industry and Saginaw Valley coal. The county today holds a mix of platted city lots, rural townships and riverfront land, each assessed by a different local office.

The county parks commission runs six parks covering more than 550 acres. Every other parcel, from a Frankenmuth storefront to a farm in Brant Township, is billed by the local unit where it lies and collected by the County Treasurer if it goes unpaid.

What should a Saginaw County seller line up before closing?

Ask your local treasurer about the current bill and the County Treasurer about earlier years, and get the payoff in writing because interest and forfeiture fees shift the total. Tell the title company if the deed will warrant title so the certificate gets ordered. The buyer then reports the sale to the assessor, and (989) 790-5270 reaches the office that files the deed.

The Treasurer and the Register of Deeds both work from the same courthouse on S. Michigan Avenue, so one trip can cover a certificate and the filing.

More questions about Saginaw County, MI Property Tax Guide

Who mails my Saginaw County property tax bill?

Your city or township treasurer mails it. Delinquent real property tax moves to the County Treasurer at (989) 790-5225.

When do Saginaw County appeals open each year?

Local boards open on the second Monday of March and keep sessions through that week. Your local assessor's office posts the exact schedule.

Is online payment available for past-due Saginaw County tax?

Yes. The County Treasurer accepts web payments at any hour through an outside vendor, for an access fee. Card payments at the counter require the named payer's government photo ID.

Will a Saginaw County sale raise the next bill?

It can. Taxable value resets to state equalized value the next year, and the buyer reports the transfer inside 45 days.

Where do I get a certificate for a Saginaw County warranty deed?

Request it from the County Treasurer in Room 107 of the courthouse, at $5 for the first five descriptions and $1 for each one after that.
